Very interesting article. A lot to chew on. A couple things that really stuck out to me. 

1. Acc to this report that the biggest risk to NVidia’s margins and profitability ironically isn’t its technology superiority eroding due to competitors catching up but rather the absolute technical dominance of its hardware-software ecosystem creating insurmountable strategic national security value and inviting more US govt direct interventions from export controls to outright margin or IP influence? Will the US govt want to take a 10% strategic stake in NVDA? 

2. Export controls have “worked” insofar as having slowed down China’s AI development. Without access to the most advanced GPUs, China has to spend time and money to reinvent key technologies that already exist in the U.S. before embarking on the multi-trillion parameters models. To Jensen’s credit, this delay isn’t free but may be bought at the expense of spurring a Chinese AI hardware-software ecosystem that’s eventually entirely independent of NVidia. That would be bad for NVidia and he argues also for the US technological dominance.

It seems that indeed may be the case bc “NVidia isn’t a car company” that’s easily substitutable but a sticky and powerful ecosystem or OS. Except to Jensen’s critics, that’s also exactly why they want to limit China’s access to it. China was always going to try to build a NVidia tech stack replica from CUDA to the interconnect software like NVLink or NIXL. Delaying China by a few months or a couple years is exactly the goal the proponents of the export controls are after. At that point, as I said in a post yesterday, the difference stems from a difference in existential values.

Bret Taylor has done almost everything in business and tech, from creating Google Maps to becoming Facebook's CTO to co-running Salesforce and now chairing OpenAI.

But there is one thing Taylor has never done, and which he says matters more than anything.

“I think the greatest achievement for an entrepreneur,” he told Reid Hoffman in 2024, “is to create a company and a brand that outlives you.”

Taylor’s first two startups, FriendFeed and Quip, were sold. Then shut down by their buyers.

His third and most recent business, Sierra, builds AI agents for large businesses to talk with their customers. He started it at 42 with his old friend Clay Bavor. Today, in a new announcement, it's being valued at over $30 billion, making Sierra the furthest Taylor has ever taken a company of his own.

So @domcooke called on Taylor at Sierra's office in San Francisco to ask whether it's easier or harder than ever to build a company that lasts, why every one of Taylor's co-founders has come from Google, and whether Sierra might complete his journey as an entrepreneur.

They also discussed his teenage years as a roadie for a ska band, how companies can differentiate in a world of agent-to-agent commerce, and how to make drinking cool again.

Enjoy this Q&A with one of the great elder statesmen of Silicon Valley, Bret Taylor.

There's tons of pros and cons to defined benefit vs defined contribution. I personally think its not all that close. I would (and do) prefer defined contribution if i were given the option.

1. as max and you already said. job mobility and portability of these plans doesn't work as its set up. Its simply not in line with the current way the job market works. 

2. Its fairly common for pensions to not include CLOA's for inflation etc. A fixed pension giving you $50k per year in 2000 is at least half as valuable as it was then.

3.  there's funding sponsor risk. There are back stops from ERISA and other things but if the company goes bankrupt that's a real potential problem and would likely lead to less money for many people in that pension plan. For public pensions its not as worrisome because they'll just increase taxes on citizens to fund it (or cut benefits from the pensioners to better balance the books)

4. Way way wayyy less flexibility. Cant change withdrawal rate. Cant change your investments to dial up or down the risk. You basically get a fixed annuity (which isn't neccessarily bad)

5. If you want that fixed annuity you can use your retirement funds in defined contribution world to buy exactly that! 

If you are going to spend the bulk of your adult life working for a stable and successful employer that will never go out of business and offers you a pension with CLOAs... that is an *excellent* retirement solution. Basically 10 out of 10. but that's a lot of "ifs" and it doesn't automatically make them the best retirement saving system for everyone or even a flexible workforce where the average person changes their job every ~5 years.

Not to mention the fact that most pensions are underfunded in the US -- much like social security.

THE DAILY METALS PULSE ⚡ | TUESDAY CLOSE • NOV 24, 2026
#Uranium #Silver #Gold #Copper

This morning I asked whether silver could reclaim $43 and gold could hold $3,600. By the COMEX settlement, silver was closer to $40 than $43, and gold had given back nearly $90 an ounce.

🥈 Silver took the hardest hit. November futures settled at $40.76/oz, down 5.5%, erasing Monday’s entire gain. Gold settled at $3,559.90/oz, down 2.4%. Gold held on to about a third of Monday’s rebound. Silver gave back every cent and another $0.28.

🔌 Copper followed silver. Shanghai’s overnight rally had been driven largely by traders covering shorts. By the New York settlement, December copper had fallen nearly 5%, more than wiping out Monday’s 2.7% gain.

☢️ One number puts the U.S. uranium supply story in perspective. Eight facilities produced uranium in Q3, yet total U.S. concentrate output fell 78% from Q2 to just 243,673 lb. The main reason was that Energy Fuels paused uranium processing at White Mesa to rebuild its ore inventory. Its next mill run targets roughly 1 million lb starting in December. That single run would produce more than four times what the entire country turned out in Q3.

🇺🇸 U.S. consumer confidence jumped to 103.3 from 91.9. The $70 billion five-year Treasury auction drew slightly softer demand, with a yield of 4.719% against 4.717% just before the sale. That was a small miss for bonds on a brutal day for metals.

Tomorrow at 8:30 a.m. ET, October PCE inflation and the revised Q3 GDP figure land together. I’m watching silver’s reaction to a softer inflation reading in particular. If yields fall and silver still struggles to hold $40, that would tell me sellers have more to unload.

Follow @Swedish_Uranium for the next Daily Metals Pulse.

Crypto is fine. We go through cycles, and wash out the bad actors with every collapse. 

Emotions can run high but the reality is the industry is stronger now than it has been at any point in the past. 

Historically we have placed far too much emphasis on short term gains, and for the first time we have multi-cycle thinkers as the focal point of the market. 

As @tulipking articulate put: either it makes money or it is money.

For the "make money" aspect, we finally have revenue producing products that people enjoy using. Obviously right now prices are lower, but good companies will weather the storm and come out the other side stronger. 

For Bitcoin: we have a lot of work cut out for us. Monetary debasement will continue, it is a fact of our financial system. Right now, rates are high and the fed is no longer the primary driver of the markets. When this changes, Bitcoin will have a narrative again. 

As always, we truck on.

Citadel said this is "2018 again".

It lays out the bear case pretty cleanly but it's not all entirely accurate. 

2018:
-> $SPY fell 19.8% from September high to 24 December. 
-> Forward P/E 16.8x -> 14.2x into the low. 
-> Q4 earnings forecasts cut from 16.6% to 12.4%. 

Today:
-> $SPY down 7.4% from October high. 
-> Forward P/E 22.0x -> 17.1x in the low.
-> Q4 earnings forecasts RAISED from 29.1% to 32.9%

We're in a very different situation in terms of growth. 

2018 was falling earnings + a hawkish Fed. 

2026 is rising earnings + a hawkish Fed. 

There's still many reasons to be cautious but my bias remains strongly on the side of the bulls.

Regarding the RTP calculation on two of our original games:

What happened:
Early in November we identified that the RTP of two of our games was not being represented correctly.

Instead of the 1% house edge being charged once at the beginning of a Risky Click or a HiLo round, it was being charged on each step. So if you cashed out after two or more steps, your payout was lower than it should have been.

The two games were some of our least popular games. Total volume across both games represents less than 1% of our total volume on original games and less than .3% of our total volume site-wide. 

After we changed the math, we had already begun the process to pay affected users.  Between some of the data for Risky Click existing on a retired and archaic RGS and the massively increased bot-swarm attacks happening across all platforms, the refunds were delayed.

That being said, we still dropped the ball, and this should have been handled much more quickly and communicated immediately that we were working on it.

When the @provablyfairorg  thread was released yesterday, our data team and development team stayed up into the early morning hours to make sure this was rectified in the shortest amount of time possible.

How the refunds were calculated:
It’s been quoted that we were charging a house edge of up to 38.89% for HiLo and 8.65% for Risky Click instead of 1%.

These numbers were the worst-case scenarios, and in practice the actual additional house edge was significantly less. For instance, for HiLo to have a 38.89% house edge, a user would have to play 49 steps in a single round, which happened zero times.

 Stated RTP: 99%
 Realized RTP: 97.82%
 After refunds: 99.69%

Risky Click:

 Realized RTP: 98.34%
 After refunds: 100.03%

Refunds were calculated on a review of every HiLo and Risky Click win of two or more steps placed on or before 10 November.

We went through every single round played where a user cashed out after two or more steps and recalculated the payouts with the updated math.

Payment:
As of last night, all refunds to active accounts have been issued. Emails have been sent stating the amounts refunded.

Self-excluded users will be sent an email with their amount owed to them, and will need to provide a wallet address for manual payment.

tweets.text: Breakdown of the RTP issue on Risky Click and Hi/Lo.
tweets.quoted_tweet_text:
Regarding the RTP calculation on two of our original games:

What happened:
Early in November we identified that the RTP of two of our games was not being represented correctly.

Instead of the 1% house edge being charged once at the beginning of a Risky Click or a HiLo round, it was being charged on each step. So if you cashed out after two or more steps, your payout was lower than it should have been.

The two games were some of our least popular games. Total volume across both games represents less than 1% of our total volume on original games and less than .3% of our total volume site-wide. 

After we changed the math, we had already begun the process to pay affected users.  Between some of the data for Risky Click existing on a retired and archaic RGS and the massively increased bot-swarm attacks happening across all platforms, the refunds were delayed.

That being said, we still dropped the ball, and this should have been handled much more quickly and communicated immediately that we were working on it.

When the @provablyfairorg  thread was released yesterday, our data team and development team stayed up into the early morning hours to make sure this was rectified in the shortest amount of time possible.

How the refunds were calculated:
It’s been quoted that we were charging a house edge of up to 38.89% for HiLo and 8.65% for Risky Click instead of 1%.

These numbers were the worst-case scenarios, and in practice the actual additional house edge was significantly less. For instance, for HiLo to have a 38.89% house edge, a user would have to play 49 steps in a single round, which happened zero times.

HiLo:
 Stated RTP: 99%
 Realized RTP: 97.82%
 After refunds: 99.69%

Risky Click:
 Stated RTP: 99%
 Realized RTP: 98.34%
 After refunds: 100.03%

Refunds were calculated on a review of every HiLo and Risky Click win of two or more steps placed on or before 10 November.

We went through every single round played where a user cashed out after two or more steps and recalculated the payouts with the updated math.

Payment:
As of last night, all refunds to active accounts have been issued. Emails have been sent stating the amounts refunded.

Self-excluded users will be sent an email with their amount owed to them, and will need to provide a wallet address for manual payment.  

What’s next?
Our number one priority still remains to be the fairest and most trustworthy place to play. To back that up, we’re rolling out a transparency and fairness program.

Don't trust us? Verify us.

This program will launch in the coming months: We will be publishing our testing methods, our simulations, and giving anyone a chance to break them. Bounties will be rewarded for any discrepancies found.

Our hope is that this motivates other platforms to lean into transparency, and makes the industry as a whole a safer place to play.

I think we’re entering an era that will disproportionately reward the curious, the resourceful, the self-taught and those who thrive in uncertainty. When intelligence becomes abundant, agency becomes scarce. That’s probably the most important thing we can cultivate in our kids now.

OpenAI has posted their own VP ≠ VNP proof in response to Anthropic's, and says their result 'was obtained on November 6, 2026.' Two weeks ago. The ETH papers were also released in an similar oneupmanship fashion. As with Anthropic's result, no name on the paper (my guess is this was GPT-Aeon). Also like Anthropic: no announcement, no blog post, no tweet. 

This is a significant result, yet both OpenAI and Anthropic chose to simply dump it online with no comment. I was listening to a Scott Aaronson interview this morning where he said this specific result would update him toward 'a solution to P ≠ NP by the AIs might really be around the corner.'
To me this is more evidence for my argument that both OpenAI and Anthropic are sitting on a dragon's hoard of scientific results they are not releasing to the public. The first massive 700+ paper OpenAI GitHub dump took five weeks for their model to generate. It's been seven weeks since then, and their internal model has continued to improve. They said they had it working on 4,000 problems. How many have been solved in the last seven weeks? Based on the last release, 1,000+ is not unreasonable.

I will quote OpenAI Chief Scientist Jakub Pachocki from the blog post 'Perplexity and Intelligence,' posted 48 hours ago:

'We have recently witnessed unprecedented acceleration in another domain. For more than a year, we have been posing open problems in mathematics to our models as one of the ways of evaluating them. Once we upgraded to a model of log-perplexity ~0.76, it started producing groundbreaking results. For many of us that have previously worked in mathematics and adjacent fields, seeing the resolutions to questions we've long thought about coming out of the model one after another in a single Slack thread felt deeply surreal.'

There have also been, of late, multiple rumors about breakthroughs in cryptography that I have been reluctant to post about for obvious reasons. Specifically, there have been rumors of an encryption breakthrough at Anthropic. What I personally took from the big OpenAI math release was that all encryption will be cracked much sooner than people are expecting, and that the rate of scientific discoveries will continually increase as we continue to scale up. No, not will increase, *has increased*. At both labs. We just don't know about it yet. Because unless you work at those labs, the current frontier is completely invisible. But it won't stay that way forever. Or to put it another way: prepare yourself for revelations.

The results in this preprint have made me update my beliefs about the future of AI in biology more than anything else I've seen so far. 

Six months ago, I would have thought that specialist models in biology would be outperforming frontier LLMs until we scale things up by another couple orders of magnitude. My median estimate for when something like this would happen would have probably been 2030. 

Instead, our generalist language models, today, are performing tasks at or above the state-of-the-art in various protein design & understanding tasks. And there is clear improvement across all domains as our models improve generally.

The implications of this are enormous - we are on the doorstep of being able to program biology using natural language.

Truly incredible work from @Masa_Uehara_1, @joyjiao12, and the team! An absolute milestone for @OpenAI and the field as a whole
